messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 21-year-old single man who works long shifts as a line chef in a busy restaurant, where the heat, noise, and constant movement leave little room to step away from himself. He was sexually assaulted several months ago after leaving work late at night. He had accepted a ride because he was exhausted and wanted to get home quickly, and what has stayed with him most sharply is not only the assault itself but the sense that control disappeared all at once. He remembers the sound of passing cars nearby while it was happening, and the presence of force in another person’s body has made any hint of violence feel charged ever since. He has come to believe that he acted in ways that go against who he is, and he says with bitterness that somebody else would have stopped it. That judgment has narrowed how he now reads the world: moments involving aggression, the sound of cars outside, or any sudden sense that he is not in control strike him as especially dangerous, as if the event has taught him exactly where threat lives. Because he was already convinced he had failed in a fundamental way, things he might once have brushed off now snagged immediately and held him—a car slowing at the curb, a coworker’s sharp movement, a stranger’s raised voice all registered faster as reminders because they seemed to confirm what he thought he had learned about himself and the world.

In the weeks after the assault, these cues began to reach him before he could think. In the restaurant kitchen, if a pan slammed down or someone cut quickly behind him, he would tense immediately, his body reacting as if something were about to happen. Even at home, a car passing outside or a raised voice on the street could make him feel on guard in his own apartment. Sudden movements by other people put him instantly on alert. Once he was in that state of alarm, the memory was harder to keep at a distance; the sheer sense of danger seemed to pull the assault back into his mind, until the sounds from that night were there again as if his body were forcing him to review what had happened. What frightened him was how little warning there was: something in his surroundings could bring the whole memory back at once, complete with the sounds he had heard during the assault, as if the scene were opening around him rather than being remembered. Once that happened, he often could not explain what had happened to him coherently; when he tried, he lost the thread and stopped talking.

The memory has become tied to the way he thinks about himself. When he starts to remember, the thought that he should have done something different comes in hard and fast, and the more he tells himself that another man would have coped better, the more the memory feels vivid and condemning. He gets stuck not only in what was done to him but in what he thinks it says about him. Those thoughts leave him feeling he has no future, and in that hopeless state the assault seems closer, more available, easier for the world to pull back into the room.

Because he feels danger so quickly, Kwame has developed rituals that make sense to him in the moment. After being startled in the kitchen or by a car outside his apartment, he checks his body repeatedly for signs of injury or vulnerability, running his hands over himself as if he might find evidence of harm he missed. At other times he tries to detach from the memories altogether, pushing them away and going blank around them. He is also ashamed of how often he imagines getting revenge on the people responsible; these fantasies come most intensely after he has been set off and is filled with the certainty that he is still not safe. For brief moments, the images of retaliation make him feel less powerless.

But these ways of coping have tightened the problem. The more he scans his body and stays braced for danger, the more readily ordinary sounds and movements register as warnings. When he tries to cut himself off from the memory, it tends to return abruptly and with more force, often with the auditory fragments intact. The revenge fantasies keep him mentally close to the assault as well, circling the same scene instead of letting it settle. He has noticed that after nights spent replaying revenge scenarios or forcing the memory away, he is even more easily jolted the next day by a car accelerating past the restaurant or a coworker moving suddenly at his side.

Over time this has changed his life at work and outside it. In the kitchen he avoids turning his back when possible and watches other people’s movements too closely, which slows him down and has led coworkers to see him as tense and irritable. At home he cannot relax. He feels alert even behind a locked door. When people ask what happened, he wants to explain but quickly becomes lost, then furious with himself for freezing again. That reaction strengthens his belief that he failed then and is still failing now. By the time he came for help, what finally alarmed him was how small his life had become and how convinced he had grown that it would stay this way. He says he wants the constant sense of danger to stop, but what he is most afraid of is that the assault has permanently changed him into someone weak, contaminated, and without a future.
